blocks.x: I'll sit down now, since we got the thing moving. Okay, let's get your name now. Julius Handy. Yeah, and let's get your name, George. Evelyn Seville. Okay, and my name is Dick Allen.

What's today's date, hmm? Oh, I think the date is the 9th, isn't it? Am I wrong? Yes, it's May the 9th. May the 9th, 1973. Yeah, okay. And where are we? What's the address? Oh, yeah, 825 North Robinson. This is a resident Julius Handy. A brother of Captain John and Sylvester Henry. Oh, I see. While we're on that, you were talking about your father a little while ago and his farm. Yeah, my dad was great. He had a band for about 17 years. He had this fellow, Tom Albers. He has passed 635 to Gunders Street when he was living. Can we stop it? I want to see if I can finish. Yeah, well, we were talking about your father's band and Tom Albers. Yes, my daddy had a band. He had the, they call it, the, what do you call it, the second line, they call it over here. They used to call it a parade over the lake with my daddy. Well, he was the place I ever had that over in Pascoe and Mississippi. Until my brother, Captain John, Henry, he passed and it was the greatest that they ever had over in Mississippi. And, uh, which he was the greatest in my eyesight. I don't know about the rest, but, uh, he and Sylvester were the greatest that I can give up to. I got to give it to Bill Summers, and he was the greatest himself. But, I mean, for, uh, brothers, I have to give it to those two because they brought me up where I am today. And, they asked me if they would pass to carry on, and I am going to carry my best.
When you mention parade and second line, do you mean that they actually, um, followed behind him when he played?

Yes, they had the other people, uh, I mean the people over there, they would, uh, follow behind my dad and his little band over there. Oh, I can't call some of the other people, that guy from over here that played with him. And, Cap, he was, just as started on clarinet. And, he come over here with Tom Albert. And, that's when he began to get with Tuck Johnson and other bands. I can't call all the names because some I know and some I don't know. And, then he finally, he got his own band. They called it the Haines, Louisiana Shakers. And, he just used to shake all over the city. Yeah, he was a great guy. He just carried everything on. So, finally, uh, Sebastian came over and he went to playing with the Tuxedas and, uh, oh, I don't know how many bands that he has played with. And, then they began to come and get me and bring me out to the Levita to Budweiser. You were still really young. I was still young then. And, they used to come and get me the nights that I wasn't playing. Well, the nights that I was playing, I was out with the real people, with the rich people. They had their parties at their own houses. And, uh, every week I had my engagements from this place to that place.
Well, you couldn't have been that young.
Well, uh, I mean, that's after I came over here.
Well, when they came to the coast they got to you, what was your age?

Mmm, I would say I was in my early parties when I came over here. One which I didn't know anyone, you know, to go play with. But, Cap, he would come get me. Sylvester, come get me. And, the guys heard about me on my little banjo. And, then I started playing with this one and that one. Then, I decided to get me a little band of my own. And, then I started at, uh, Miss Bernice, I'm Roman and Palmeyer. What was that? Miss Bernice, Roman and Palmeyer. I started playing there. They used to call it the Madame Priest Bill Paul. And, I started playing there, well, I hired Kid Clayton. Oh, I played with, he played with me a long time. And, Billy and Dee, Billy and Dee Dee, they was my honeys. Dee Dee was my trumpet player. And, Billy was my piano player. And, uh, finally, I hired, uh, uh, I can't think of his name. He's a drummer for the Old, no, he isn't a drummer for the Old India Band. I'll call his name in a minute. I've done, there's so many musicians on my mind. I can't call his name right now. Who did they play? This, uh, his son played drums, played snare drums, and he played the bass. Booker T. Yeah, well, he's with the Atlanta. Right, uh-huh. Well, Booker T was my drummer. And, that was a little before his son started right off playing. And, uh, it was amusing, you know. And, it's still amusing to know the musicians that has played with me. And, the phone numbers, I had my little book now. I doubt if any of them remember the phone numbers, you know, that, uh, I used to call him. Like Chester Jones. I know he wouldn't think of the number that I had, you know, old time number. Alvin Alcon. He was there. And, uh, Teddy Riley. I got my kicks out of him. I can't play this. I can't play that. I said, Teddy, you can play it. He was a youngster. I said, just try. And, I admire him now because he gives me all the credit for him being out on Burbank Institute today. Oh, that's marvelous. He does. And, I mean, it's great, you know, when, uh, someone, when you do them, when you do something for them. And, they acknowledge you. Right. And, they acknowledge you. I mean, and every time, I heard it the other night. Okay. A guy came by here and he told me, he said, you, he says, yeah. He said, you know Teddy Riley? I said, well, that's my little buddy. He says, every time I talk with him, he said, you would have called him being out on Burbank Street because he didn't want to play that.
What was his name? Trumpet. Trumpet. Mm-hmm.

Yeah, a little carnet he was playing and he doubted himself, you know. And, I told him, forget about it. Don't doubt you, he said, just go right along and, like for me, I don't care what banjo player they have out there, I'm going to do what I know how to do. Somebody's going to like my playing. So, forget about the next guy. Finally, you may be getting, you may get to be greater, as great, or greater than he. So, I never, my daddy taught me, don't try to imitate anybody else on your instrument. Just go ahead and play. Well, that's good advice to anybody on this guy's playing.
Yeah.
Take it like Dick. He tried to imitate me talking, oh, he'd be way out, he can't make it. And, I couldn't go along with him with him, you see.
So. Different strokes for different folks. That's right.
Well, I am, they all tell me everywhere that I'm the loudest fan here player in the city. Which I go along with them. Because, my daddy taught me a certain way.
Does that have anything to do with strength? No, it doesn't.

It doesn't have anything to do with strength. It's all in the things that you put on your strings. All in the things that you put on your strings. But, outside of that, the stroke, it doesn't have anything to do with it. Because, I can take my band right now, and I can get a stroke, and I can choke my strings, and you just can hear it. It's something like, that mic, if you don't know how to turn the mic on, it'll squeak or squeal. Right. If not, it's going to be too low. So, it's just one of those things that you learn and you keep in mind, you see. I used to get my kicks out of Sylvester and Kath. When was about when you were in the next year? No, I was about fourteen years old. We used to go out over the lake. And we had three cousins. They had played banjo, I mean ghetto, mandolin, and clarinet. Well, we played ghetto, mandolin, and Sylvester, he was on my daddy's bass. Well, we used to go out around the lakefront. And those big houses where the rich people was, around 8.30 or 9 o'clock, we'd go up on their porch and we'd start playing. They'd come out to give us a dollar a piece or five dollars, you know, to divide between the three of us. When we finished up, we may go home at that time. Twenty-five dollars was a million dollars at that time. Oh, God. And guess how much we would get out of it? Fifteen or twenty cents a piece if we got that much. Why? Well, we brought it home to our mother and dad.
Those were long ago days.

Well, I'll tell you what. I'm proud of that today because my daddy told us, if I start you off with two dollars, and I get so I can't give it to you, and you're not able to go out there and make it, there's something else going to happen. You have to get it somewhere. And that's what happens to a bunch of teenagers today. The parents started them off too early. I gave them fifteen dollars, ten dollars. I know some children in my life right now, every week they got to get three or four dollars. Now, when the parents can't give it to them and they're only five or six years old,
That makes a lot of sense.

When the parents can't give it to them, well, they're going to give it to them. They feel the pride, right. And I appreciate that today because any time we kept clean, we kept with nice clothes on that kept us just like we were supposed to be, but not with a pocket full of money, but anything we thought we needed. We said, my daddy, he believed in a lot of food. And that's where Sylvester got that from. When Sylvester was here, they didn't. You go back to his house, he had too much food.
So he wasn't fat, wasn't he? How did I?

He wasn't fat. No, no, no. Oh, he didn't eat that much. He just believed in that when people come to his house, when, just had to cook and just come on and eat. And so, well, that's where our dad is. My mother and my daddy brought us up. Excuse me. And I like my sister. We have one sister. And she's a dog. And my mother, she was a pianist. I mean, we all, the whole family is musical in the club. And my sister, she plays all of them. And she said she played piano for church.
And your cousins played. So which side of the family did they connect you to?
Those cousins, well, they passed.
Were they from your mother's side?

No, no, they were from my daddy's side. Distant cousins from my daddy's side. And, well, we were, from what I know, I knew more about the family in a way than Sylvester and Cal. They were just other school and go. Well, I hate to say it, well, I can't help it. But I'm a polio victim. I never did work. My daddy didn't want me to work. He didn't want me to get married. And he, they just, anyway, everywhere my daddy had gone, I had to be right there. And, uh.
No, you're catching it.

Mm-hmm. So what happened, that's why I know more about the family than Sylvester and Cal because they were just happy-go-lucky. When they get finished working, they just, my daddy let them go. But everywhere he went, I was right there. Come on, get on the wagon and go with me. Or come go this place. Or come, he was amusing me. He didn't allow me to wrestle. He didn't allow me to do this. That's the only thing I see. I wish they should have did. Oh, not change one for the other though.
No, no.

I suppose he hadn't been so interested in the music. That wasn't the idea. That wasn't the idea. It was the idea of letting me exercise more. You understand? But he kept me with that music. And he bought, uh, piano. Every time I turned around, I would bang, on the piano.
Did you hear Dick just then?
I did. He's great. Thank you.
He was trying to convince me that was a whole piece.

I was bang, bangin' on the piano. Well, there's one thing I will give my daddy. He never did say that annoy me. Don't do this and don't do that. I used to hear a clap, uh, Cap. Used to make me angry. Blang, with the clarinet, you know. I said, I wish my daddy would stop it. But he knew that's how he had to learn. He let Cap do the same thing. He let Sylvester do the same thing.
Well, none of y'all had instructions other than from your father.

Well, no. Uh, we came up, and by his plane, and, uh, from out of town, we had, uh, Professor Randolph in Meridian, Mississippi. He had, uh, the old professor, he had a school at my home where we used to go to. And his son had, he was a principal of a big school in Meridian, Mississippi. And he came down and he heard us play. And he asked my daddy to let us come up in Meridian at Haven Institute.
All three of you at the same time? All three of us at the same time. I thought there was a larger age difference, though.
No, no, no. And so, my dad and my mother, they agreed for us to go. So finally, he told my mother and my dad, no tuition for them. Whenever they have anything at the school, they said,
they were paying their tuition. And we would teach them through school, plus their music.
Isn't that one?

And we didn't have anything to pay. And it would have kicked out, but I was the youngest on the campus. It amused me because they had, sometimes they'd have onions and grits. And I'd look at it and I'd get up, but I was so used to, my mother and dad had anything we wanted to eat, I'd never say no, I don't want that. And they'd take me to the table about me being the youngest in the whole bunch. Over there, where they were eating liver and this and that.
When young, you're talking about around 10 or younger than that?
I was around 12.
12, so the boys were up in their teens.

Yeah, uh-huh, yeah. So when Sylvester was talking about, they were living in the dormitory. And sometimes they'd let me go to the dormitory with Sylvester and Sylvan, and most of the time I'd stay at the residence, you know, stay at their house. But it was amusing. Well, Dick, what did you play?
For me, just now? I just played blues.
I just played blues. Yeah, I heard it. I didn't know what that was.
Part of it sounded a little familiar. Did it sound good? Part of it sounded to me. It sounded like, um, what did I say at the side?
I can't remember, but no.
What have they done to my song? That's what it meant.
What I wanted to know is, what were the real birth dates of you and your brother? Do you know? Well, Dick... That you know more about your family than...

I'll tell you. My mother and my dad, they had, like my little group there, they had, uh... they had a Bible. in the head. My first day, they had Sylvester's, and they had Jones. Pardon me. Well, I always was, as far as the Bible, I was three years younger than, uh, Sylvester. And Sylvester was two years younger than 10. So, by the census, you know, they'd gone along with it and they'd changed it. You know what I mean? Mm-hmm. So, I mean, there's nothing that we can go on, go about. Mm-hmm. Uh, just like they... When I sent for my birth certificate, I had to sign this and go through this and go through that. When they went to, uh, Washington, D.C., they sent me back my birth certificate. Well, I'm just here. They didn't have no record of me. They didn't know where I came from. But they gave you the date. Yeah, I have. Yeah, they gave me my date and everything. And, uh, so, well, I mean, that's the only thing. I can go by. But, uh, just like for my daughter and my son now, their mother had their, uh, records and the Bible and everything. And they had their birth certificate.
Right.

They wanted to go through all that. No. But at that time, we didn't have a birth certificate. Long time ago, when they had a flood over there, but that took all our funnages, Bible, and everything. And so, that's the way it was then. Well,
it was 1900 or what? What was right?
1915. They had a big, uh, storm. No, I mean,
your actual birthday, birth year.
1907. 1907. But they had me 1904.
Oh. And what's your birthday?
February 15th.
Mm-hmm. And then what would Syl's birthday be?

Uh, I just remember what, uh, I know Captain June, and I can't think if Sylvester was in October, or exactly when, which I can't tell what month my sister, I think my sister was in May. I'm hungry. Because I'm, because I'm, because I'm, because I'm, and sometimes I call my, I call my ex-wife sometime, and I say, uh, how old is Junior? So you don't have to be saying, because I say, well, I don't know.
What about your father? We were talking about him and his violin, and his band and all.

You're telling us about his violin. Well, my daddy had a violin, and, uh, no violin he had. The people that gave him this other violin, they said it was 150 years old. It had a good sound, it was a wonderful instrument. The, the weight of it, you know, showed how much, uh, and, uh, someone told my daddy about how you can make a violin sound. And he told my daddy to get a rattlesnake, rattler. My daddy got two rattlesnake rattlers, and he put those two rattlesnake rattlers in the get to, I mean, in the, in the violin. And you can't imagine how much vibration. It sounded like some of these violins that sound so far. It was great. It's marvelous. It is.
But you must really have to want a rattle to go out and get a rattle, snitch, rattle.

I don't want snitch through it myself. I'm afraid of it. But, uh, he didn't go out and get it. I don't know, someone brought him, brought it to him, gave it to him. But he wasn't afraid of the rattle. I used to look at it and he used to say, boo, to me, you know, with it, you know, and I'd run and he'd get a kick out of me running from the rattle because he knew I was afraid of snakes. But, uh, that thing sounded, now you have to let it dry. You can't just take the rat from the rattle and put it in the bottom. You have to let it dry dry. And not a lot of people
did this, right? Just, um...
Well, that's the first I've ever known. I didn't know it then. And then, after then, I heard several people
doing it. Right. Dick had heard it. Who did you know that did that for a rattle? Well, I've heard
about country fenders in the... all over the country. I never heard of people in the city but I think it's known throughout the country.

I said, well, that happened over the lake and I never will forget it because it was so amazing to hear how loud the difference in how loud his violin sounded. I wish I had that violin today. Now, I have a banjo that, uh, the fellow used to play with my dad. He used to play a banjo with my dad. It was his banjo. And his son let me have a banjo. And, uh, it's amazing. You've been strong
for a long day?
Just to look at it. I haven't even had a head put in it. It's interesting about that long. But it's, uh, it's a vega, dick? Oh, really? It's a vega, yeah.
Who is this man? The dad?
His name was Joseph Sosche. Joseph Sosche. He played trumpet with my daddy. Then he had another father. His name was Edgar Sosche. He played trumpet with my daddy for a long time.
And, uh,

it was amusing, you know, just to come up in the musical family. Of course. That's quite prevalent. Now, where I used to get my kicks showing up, when I began to learn my banjo a little more, Jeanette Kimbrell, she was a Jeanette Seliborne, but Jeanette Kimbrell, they had a movie picture show. We used to call it movie picture show, not a theater. We used to call it movie picture show. And, uh, Jeanette used to play in between the pitches. It was, it was a silent pitch. It wasn't, you know, and in between the pitches when they get ready to change the radio, and then Jeanette used to play. Well, what, and you and me, so, when I used to get such kicks out of it, Jeanette used to tell me, Julius, why don't you bring your banjo and come play with me? And, uh, I'd get a kick out of it because I wouldn't have the pain to go in. You actually did. And didn't know that it was, uh, enlightening me more on my instrument, you understand? All I was enthused of is not paying a little dime or fifty cents to go in. She was pretty well. Oh, she's cute. She's cute. She's a honey. And, uh, she and, uh, Marguerite Booth, she's in Oakland, California now. Well, uh, they played piano on the same title, and they were great. And she met...
she was playing on the coast in the movie, uh, I don't know, or, or,
Hayden Royce.

No, Wilming Paster's Town. She was. Uh-huh. And, uh, in between that, well, they, uh, she began to, well, she was a pianist, and I was just a beginner trying to learn bandwale, but I learned a lot from her, just by me going, called myself, playing just to be in the show, going to the show. But I didn't, I couldn't imagine... That wasn't your incentive. It wasn't your incentive. They were doing me so much good, you know? Right. And so, uh, I mean, it was great. I mean, you can do so many little things, you don't know, and you don't know what it's doing good for you. But Jeanette, she was great, and she's still great. I admire her a lot, because, uh, nah, for the banjo part, I give John Gantle credit, because, when Cap would come over to Lake, he was over here a good while. When he'd come over to Lake with Sam Argan, or any other band, he'd come over to Lake. He just adored me. I was just his, uh, alive. When Cap come over, I didn't know too much about banjo, or this or that, and those guys came over, they knew what they were doing. And Cap shoots to tell him, I got my little brother can play banjo, make him cut you in. So, Cap would tell him what key to play in. The Sam Argan, he'd play maybe in G, where I probably maybe could just make that same G all the way through. But it made me get more further than I was. Well, when Jack came over, come over with Cap, and then they'd come over, they'd come over maybe three or four hours earlier. And when they'd come to my house, my daddy had a big dinner for some time, the whole band would come there and eat. And Josh Ganner, I admired him all the way up to the day.
He really took time.

He took his time, and he would sit down with me and teach me this part, and teach me that part. Little dad, they had a, you remember Little Daddy? Yes. Little dad, he used to come over with Sam Argan, come over with this band or that band. Well, they all knew me through capital. And they'd come over. Where's Little Henry? The one who played banjo, I want to cut his head. They would be teasing me, you know, but they would take me and teach me. Guy, yeah, he would do the same thing.
Well,
they must have seen
something we had to want to work with.

Yeah. And, well, Kimberl, his daddy used to play with Celestan, the original Celestan, used to play bass. Finally, Kimberl started playing banjo. And Kimberl took up a lot of time with me. Do you understand? Did you know
about Kimberl's daddy playing bass? Yeah,
yeah,

I've seen pictures of him and heard about him, Kimberl and many other men. Well, youngster, and they coming over there, you know what I mean? Then by Cap, when he came over here, well, they just jumped over him. He was just crazy with that climate because Cap didn't want to go back over there cutting no more wood with my daddy. So he just playing with some of his own, see? And it was great. It was great. And I still love the musical world. Because I don't think he can find anything any better. But the old man upstairs, because, while he's playing music, I always would have said this. It didn't say that you're not a Christian or that you are not this, you are not that. It's in this little thing inside. If that heart is right, and you write, and you're not old man, it's straight up above, that's what counts. Because he said, make, how do you say that? Make a joyful noise? No, make your money by the sweat of your eyes. and when you're playing music, don't you think that you're just sitting there playing. You press fine, and I mean, you're just as wet as you can be. I used to take my brother Sylvester. Oh, he used to take it so until when he finished playing. I used to tell him, I said, Syl, why don't you take the sweater and put it on? No, he don't know sweat. He walk off. I mean, something wet. Well, that's from the sweat of your eyes.
That's also a lot of fun.

It was something three weeks, three weeks or two and a half weeks before Sylvester passed. He didn't want to eat, and he just thought I should be right there by him. He called me, his wife called me, Jews, I said, yes, she said, Sylvester said, you haven't been out here to see him in a week. She said, you could go out here Sunday and it's only Tuesday. I said, well, she said, June, I can't get Sylvester leave. Would you do me a favor? I said, I do you a favor him too. She said, well, it's 730 now. How soon can you get out here? I said, I'll be out here in a little while. She said, have you had breakfast yet? I said, no. She said, well, I have bacon, I have ham, I have egg, I have grits. And she says, when you come, you mention what you want to eat for breakfast. Because I'm going to ask you do you want breakfast. And you say, yes. ! I said, yes, I what? I said, oh, hazel. She said, what, you have you eaten that? I said, no. I said, I'm hungry now. She said, what do you want? I said, get me some bacon. I said, I want any bacon. Give me ham, eggs and grits. How about some hot biscuits. I said, you have coffee? She said, yes. She

She said, I don't want y'all to come back here. She brought it in, you know, where he could see it good. He sat there, he looked at mine. Well, honey, she said, yeah, yeah. Fix me a breakfast like Jews have. Oh, she turned and she looked at me and she winked. I said, I don't fix him anything. Who bought that? I said, you did. And he ate. He went out and started playing checkers. And he said, Jews. I said, yes. He said, sir. I want to ask you something. I want you to do something for me. I said, like what? He said, if you be the longest liver. He said, wait a minute. He pulled this one down. Oh, honey. She said, yes, sir. She said, come here. He said, come here. She went, she come out there. He said, what you doing? He says, listen to this. She said, what, Jews? I said, I don't know. He said, you. He said, if you be the longest liver, I want a second line. I said, you will get it, sir. He says, I said, if you be the longest liver, I want a second line. He said, I see that you get it. Well, sure enough, he passed. He said, I want a second line. I want a second line. I want a second line. I want a second line. I want a second line. I mean, it made me feel so good to know, you know, that I was in a position. To see the next line. Well, which I call the guys. And it was great. Dick, you were there, weren't you?
I was at the wake. I had to work the next day. But I was there when we talked to Claiborne about getting together, the guys, you know, for the day. Yes. At the wake. It was amusing.
How many years between Sylvester's death and John's death?
Uh, about a year. Because John certainly had a nice send-off. John, his wife, and then he said, about a year and a half between those.
Did you help organize John, sir?
How the?
Did you help organize John's?
No, no. I'm not sure. I think I did that.

Yeah, this is the second reel of Sylvester Hand. Do you want to get to it? Yes. Okay. Yeah, we were talking while she's gone about how the camp funeral got organized. Well, the main people that helped with all that were Fred and Philly. Right. Yeah, quite.

As far as I know, because I was so much in grief until I didn't know what was going on. All I did, it was so amusing to me to see so many people and to see you and different other you know, that, uh, but, uh, but, uh, they had, uh, see at the funeral, that's the first time, those people that had a band to come into church. Mm-hmm. And if you're a band, they come right on, if, you're a band, they come right on in the church playing. Yeah. Do you understand? Do you understand? Like they usually do. Mm-hmm. And now, just like when Bob Brand died, the Catholic people didn't allow, I mean, they didn't allow Bainan to come into the church. Do you understand? Well, Bob Brand was Catholic, but they didn't let the people come into the church. So now, as far as you being a Protestant or Presbyterian or something like that, if you weren't Catholic, you could pass a body in front of a Catholic church all the time, the bell wouldn't turn. Do you understand? But by Cap's wife, she being such a great Catholic, and she was so great over the lake, and he was great himself. And when they hit the railroad track and got in front of the church, which was about three or four blocks over, had some people noticing that the body was passed in front of the church. And they started turning the bell, and that's the first time those people over the lake ever known and ever heard of that. And every church that he passed in front of, white and colored, the bell turned. Isn't that powerful? And they passed his body back in front of the house, and come all the way back around, and hit second street and went to the cemetery. And the band was wonderful. They played from the church all the way to the cemetery.
About how far?
Oh, see, about, I was about a mile, a little further. And neither part of it. They didn't know anything about second line and recently.
You don't have to know when you get involved in something like that. You're in it.

They're coming back from the cemetery. They were like, you're in it. I don't know what number that is struck into. But they had some of the real second lines from over here that had gone over there because they had free buses and everything. And all you could see, the umbrellas jumping and tearing up in trees on top of houses and this and that. And so, one of the high sheriffs over there said, I was one of the biggest students that they ever had in the state of Mississippi. Which I believe in.
Of course.
Because they had people from all over.

And they used to see you get too high and wouldn't know where you live. All that in there, they didn't sleep. Ain't nobody no body. I mean, there wasn't anyone body.
No, it's true. You can't say that today.

No, you couldn't do that today. But, uh, they had, uh, this fellow Frank Toad, he used to be around by my daddy all the time. I used to come to my daddy's house and my daddy used to have rehearsal. That's why, uh, Punchfield's got to be so good. My dad used to call rehearsal twice a week. And, uh, well, they didn't, he didn't worry about Tom after rehearsing because, uh, when Tom would come over, my daddy would tell him, you know, what number they would rehearsal, this number, that number. And, uh, he'd sit around. He'd always lead that three or four hours, you know, before time. Because, uh, he'd come on the train. Well, they didn't have, uh, say, and time if the train would leave from here and go over to New Orleans. I mean, to the pass. If he'd wait for the next train, he'd be too late to get on the job with my daddy, you see.
How long did it take to get from New Orleans to the pass that way?

I think about two hours. Two hours, maybe two hours and a half. And that's not bad, really. No. Well, nah, I mean, the best they are now. It still takes almost an hour. Nah, you take... I see so many people make it from over here in a car, 45 minutes. And some make it an hour. And when I leave, if it's two hours, it's alright with me now because I don't be in all that big a hurry. Right. But some, so many of them now, you'll find they turn upside down on the highway. And since they build this high at 10, I'd rather go to the old highway than go to the high at 10 now because they go too fast. Now, did you know, oh yeah, you had this guy's name? Oh, I can't call his name. I can't call his name. Because there's so many guys that I played with here since I've been here. And so many of them has passed, you know.
Where was the guy from and what did he do?

Yeah, I mean him. Did he work with animals? Yes, indeed. Because a lot of jobs I would get. And I called him to play piano with him. And then jobs he would get, he'd play piano and I would play banjo. I'd like to see Hood. I hadn't seen him in so long. I don't know whether he's still alive or what. And uh, Eddie Johnson, I played with him a lot of times. Which Eddie Johnson? Eddie Johnson. He died a couple of years back. What did he play? Saxophone. You talking about big head Eddie? The work at work? Right. Right. Right. Right. Yeah. That one. That one. Yeah. That one. Yeah. That one. That one. That one. Yeah. Yeah. And then I played with Sidney Cates. Oh, right. What was Cates playing? Cates was playing banjo. Oh, you had two banjos or banjo and get all? Yeah. Well, sometimes we played. Sometimes we played banjo and get all. Oh, I see. Yeah, Sidney Cates, I worked with him. Would that be a full ban or would that just be the two of them? No, it would be a full ban. I see. It would be a full ban. Because sometimes he didn't feel like going on the job and he'd play a while and he'd say, look at him, he'd say, I'm going to sleep off, I'm going home. Yeah. Because he was a carpentry too, you know. Right.

Yeah. Well, so many of these fellows you're mentioning are two instrument players. Is this usual that they would have two instruments that they played? Well, yeah. Sometimes they'd have two banjos. No, I'm talking about, like for instance yourself, your banjo and guitar, the solo was piano and trumpet. Was this common that most musicians had at least two instruments that they played? Yeah, it was common. You see, a piano and a banjo, a piano and a guitar.

That was more appropriate because it was more of a background. That was your string instrument, you know. Bass, piano and a guitar. That was the string instrument. You had to know chords. Yeah, you had to know your chords. You had to know the chords. What kind of dances did people do, by the way, when you were coming out? They did the black bottom and they did the two step. And one step. And they had the one step. And they had the one step. They had the waltzes. And then they had the shardis, they used to call it. That was a slower dance than the waltzes, you know. And well, you had to know how to play all that too. Right now, you couldn't get anyone that unless it would be an elder fellow that knows how to play a shardis. Then plenty of them don't know how to play a waltz. You say, I don't hear waltz anywhere you go. You say, I don't hear waltz. I don't hear waltz. I love to hear waltz. I love to hear waltz. I love to hear him because... but this other color that has his band. He was down here not too long ago. Long as well? Long as well. I love to hear him because...
He's strong on waltzes.

That's right. I mean, he's... And then we used to play a melody of waltzes. In other words, like the All of My Dream, we'd play that in a waltz, we'd play this, and so many waltzes, you know, just one right behind another. They used to play, people used to dance waltzes for... The best dancer would get a cake. And then they had the cakewalk. Used to play the cakewalk. And at that time, if you eat a cake, piece of cake at that time, when the old people used to make, if you had a cake. And he used to play the cakewalks, and the shatters, and the dates and that. I mean, it was something... A little variety. Well, it was for you to go to a dance too, because now, just like when they had this... Black Bottom, and this Charleston, and all like that. I mean, they used to dance for primes. It's like the capes, and this...
Well, it has to be easier for a musician to change his pace, and go on to the different types, rather than sticking to one set, then all night.

It is. But now, it's just like, for me, I go out there and play the street, and say, come on, Julius, and play a number with us. Well, if I'm not used to that type of music, we say, no, I am. It's no sweat for me. But I go out there with a bunch of rock and roll. Julius, come on, play a number. I don't feel good tonight. I don't feel like playing, because I know I'm not going to qualify with them, and they're not going to be qualified with me. So no need of me getting up there, and I know I'm not going to do right, because everybody lies on the musician when they get up on the stand. And I say to myself, I know I ain't no giving self-paste because no need of me getting up there. But to get out there, go to Crazy Shirley's, and any of those places, where any of those bands playing out there, I know I can fit in, you understand? But just for me to get out there, and now some of them know that they may play, but I haven't played in a long time. I might make it miss a few chords, just until it, but before I play too long, it's going to all come back to me. Yeah. And uh...
What about, did you ever play in any dining rooms, or restaurants, or anything like that?

I used to play behind uh, uh, those synth, the orchestras used to uh, am I saying right? Mm-hmm. To come to the auditorium? Mm-hmm. Well uh, Mr. Leon Garccio, I played so many parties, and he had uh, they had a big uh, to do that hotel lab. He called me, he said, Julius, I said, he said, come by the uh, Roosevelt. He said, come to somewhere, he told me, come by the bar, I want to talk with you. Well, they had one of those big things going on over there, I said, nah, he wants six pieces, I don't know how to do that. I thought my, my men was gonna take cold feet, you know, because that big band, it was a hundred and four, or two or three pieces, you know. And uh, so, the band had the people so bored, you know, just playing, and the auditorium was packed like that. Mr. Leon had us in the back, and he said, Julius, I said, yeah. you all better come on and get a drink, so you all can uh, you won't feel bad going behind that band out there. I, well, we got bored with the band out there, so, I'll be, I'll be glad we got started. So, we went out there, so we sit there, we drink, and, we got out there, all the people just, he had announced, you know, that he had his band coming out there, and the people just carried on, and we woke everybody up that was in there, woke everybody up that was in there, I mean, it was something. and, and, then, used to play a lot of the parties at the Roosevelt, I used to play some of the parties at the, uh, at the, uh, jump, and what this hotel might be, or what, yeah, I played a lot of parties out there, and then, uh, I used to live out there playing, but they had a turntable, they think they had a turntable, you know, where y'all is, especially when I'm in the band going, right, right, I know that. and, and I played a lot of people in, stuff like stuff

You remember this baseball park used to be out there? Tynalyn Park? Yeah. I used to be out there a lot too. Pelican Stadium they called it Lady Air. Pelican Stadium, yeah. I used to play with all of them.
Did you ever play any hotels on the Gulf Coast?
Yeah.
What were some of the big hotels over there?

Mexican Gulf Hotel that was in the past. Univista Hotel was in Biloxi. Oh practically all those hotels in Biloxi, I played that. I never forget one night we played, we played a private party in the past. And they brought Cal Sylvester and I to, told us to come take a ride. Well we had to make them bring us home, find out for my daddy. My daddy said, you all being responsible for my boys. He said, because I'm crazy about my boys. So they said, we gonna take care of them. We go all up and down on the Gulf Coast, Gulf Coast and we get in Biloxi.
It was about one o'clock.

You all better come on in here and let's go in here and get something to eat. I looked up at Cap. Cap looked at me and said, what are we gonna do? Cap said, we can't walk home. He said, let's go on in here. We got to the door. They let all them in. He said, they can't come in. One of the fellas, boy, had gone in while we were outside and ordered everything, dinner for all of us. And they told them we couldn't come in.
Why was it that you weren't allowed here?
Well, they didn't lie to call it in there sitting there eating. Oh, of course, of course.
I thought they were talking about you all were too young to be in some way.

No, no, no. They didn't lie to call it to come in there and eat. And so they told them to cancel the dinner. So this guy went and told the big man. And the big man, he came there and he said, sure. He said, let them in. We sit there and we played. And these people was from, some of them were from California. Some were movie stars and all like that. And so we started playing. They asked the people we were with, asked the big man, said we play a few numbers. And they said, sure. And the people started throwing money all on the floor. And the first time I ever seen that in my life, a guy had a book, something like this. And he could tell his dollars and hundred dollar bills out of the books, out of that book, you know. And he says, don't either one of you all get up and pick up a penny on that floor. If they don't think enough of you to bring it and give it to you, he says, don't take it. I took all that money on the floor.
That was by advice, wasn't it?

I took all that money on the floor. Well, that was just a fee, you know. So we went on and left it on the floor. And Cap, he was saying with the people, after we got home now, we was finished with the people. After we got home, Cap, he went to fussing to himself with us. Somebody picked up those pennies. Somebody in his mind. Sure, somebody picked it up. Pennies, quarters, nickels and all like that all over the floor. Cap, he was talking about how much money that we could have had if he'd have let us pick it up, you know.
You know, the person that was selling you that had a big old wallet full of money.
Well, sure. Sure, he had his. He didn't have anything to worry about. He was a movie star, but I mean, I don't know his name. He was just a great guy.
What was Mardi Gras like over there when you were growing up?

Mardi Gras was one of them. In other words, they had a fellow by the name of Albert Alexander. And he had a little group there and they used to build floats and all like that. And we used to play on the floats just like they did here. But I mean, it was just a smaller group and everything. But every year they'd have about, if they didn't have but two, it was a big mardi Gras for us. Well, I remember hearing tales about Pastor Candy and that. We had two or maybe three floats and people always did have a wonderful time over there. Oh, I agree with you. I used to love. They know how to live on the coast.
Right.

And you see in the evening, you get ready to come back over there after the excourging. They used to have waiters like, and they'd be about that square each way. And they'd have great big fish sandwiches. More fish than they could hardly get between the braids. And potato salad.
If you really can't imagine. Things changed so quickly over there. That's right.
And potato salad. Yeah.
But it was a whole different way of moving than any other part of the salad.

Right. Ten and fifteen cents, they'd be holding them up at the wind there at the train, which you can't open the windows now. The windows used to be open. And they'd hold them up and people buying like, I don't know what, some people would buy enough just to bring home too. And fish, they'd catch them that morning and try them that evening and have them out there waiting for the people coming back over here. Yeah, it was something great. And, uh.
Did they have kings and queens balls or anything? Yes.

Or was it just a matter of a parade? No, they had a parade and the kings and queens and they had all that. I mean, it was just like it was over here. In other words, to us, it was more great over there to us than it was here. It was there? Yeah.
Did you ever play for the balls there?

Yes, indeed. They had, uh, Central America School and the church and, uh, I used to play for the churches and schools and, uh, any one of them would, in other words, I was one of the, uh, biggest guys that they'd hire, you know, to play for this and play for that. White school, colored schools and dances and this and that. I wish I could call back some of those days.
Oh, I wish I could have been a part of some of those days. Yes. I came up in the wrong generation. I'd like to...

I was saying the other day, I wish I had, uh, some of the, uh, and I like, used to get so much good fish over there. Now, this water began to, you know, gather in this and do this and do that. And you can't get all that now. The crabs, you can't get that. The shrimp, you can't get all that. And, uh, Sylvester Cap and I, we used to walk out to, like, from here to Claiborne Street. In between, they'd have that, uh, they'd have the, what you call it? Uh, they'd have the, the sand beds. The what? Sand beds, they used to call it. Sand beds. In other words, like, you could walk from here to here. Oh, I was just saying. Right. And they wouldn't have it and they'd have sand here, you see. Right. And you'd get ready to walk from here, it would be water about up to your ankle, maybe to your knee, and over there it would be sand. You could keep on walking around. Yeah, uh-huh, well in between there, they used to have crabs like that.
Just walk along with scoogamabots.
Just walk along and, uh, we'd take sticks and catch them. And, uh, sometimes Calc and Sylvester would come home with a whole cycle.
Toes work just as well, too. Uh-huh. Toes work just as well.

Yeah, uh-huh, right. And, uh, it was so wonderful. And I liked shrimp. You could walk over there. Over there you could walk out there and pick up, uh, my daddy used to walk from water up to here. And they had a little net. He used to make those nets. And throw out there and shoot, he'd come back with a whole big, half a sack of shrimp, and great big shrimp.
Uh-huh, uh-huh. And at night, my daddy used to go clowning.
With a torchlight?
With a torchlight and a spear.
And you see big clowners like that, big clowners like that. I used to see—
Well, you still see kids doing that during the night.

Yeah, I used to ask my daddy to let me, uh, I said, let me get it. Boy, that thing will drown you in that water. He said, you hit him down, you hit him with that spear, you wouldn't be heavy enough to hold him. And he'd get out from underneath there. And, uh, that's good eating. This clowners.
